A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BuildArena research. Their complete text, tables, figures, mathematical definitions, and appendices support comparison; the retained material can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v5 reports original simulation results for nine LLMs across nine task-level combinations, plus workflow ablations, decoding sensitivity, and closed-loop refinement experiments.

after.justification: v7 retains those original results and adds open-weight model evaluations, prompting comparisons, analyst-assisted refinement, complex constructions, and quantitative library-fidelity measurements.

M1.justification: The main five-role construction workflow and geometric library remain unchanged. Appendix D introduces an analyst agent for an additional Lift closed-loop procedure: it examines structures, simulator feedback, and trajectories using code/file tools, then appends improvement suggestions to subsequent prompts.

E1.justification: The three task families and their original difficulty levels are retained. Figure 11 and Appendix J.2 add a Tower Bridge-inspired construction scenario requiring towers, a suspended deck, and architectural complexity, extending task requirements within the existing bridge domain.

E2.justification: The evaluated model set expands from nine to twelve through Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-27B, and Ministral-14B, each evaluated across all nine task-level combinations in v7 Table 4. This substantially expands model comparisons; the original models and workflow-ablation comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v7 substantially extends evaluation procedures with a controlled zero-shot/one-shot comparison, a five-round analyst-assisted Lift experiment, and a 49-step library-versus-simulator check. Section 2.4 also reclassifies part count from a lower-is-better performance metric to a descriptive measure and specifies ranking by success rate and indicator. Original task prompts, decoding parameters, and simulator settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test demonstration sensitivity (Table 3), analyst-assisted recovery on Lift (Table 9), whether prompts permit more complex constructions (Figure 11), and geometric fidelity to Besiege (Figure 12). These materially broaden validation beyond the retained workflow ablations, decoding study, and Support refinement case.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 64-sample averaging, the 18-failed-sample Support refinement study, and the mean-plus-standard-deviation display in Figure 8. New experimental tables follow the existing averaging practice; no new seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: The original performance, cost, workflow-ablation, decoding, and Support-refinement table values are unchanged. Substantial new results include GPT-5 Support Lv.1 success of 85.9% under zero-shot versus 65.6% under one-shot prompting, Qwen3.5-27B's 35.9% Support Lv.1 success, and DeepSeek-3.1's 3.1% Lift Lv.2 success at analyst-assisted Round 4. Appendix F.5 additionally reports very small geometric discrepancies.

T1.justification: Appendix F retains the same construction-state, module, pose, control-sequence, and action-trajectory definitions. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised; the new fidelity check is empirical.

C1.justification: The benchmark, extensible task design, and geometric-library contributions remain intact. v7 narrows the introduction and conclusion toward construction-stage spatial assembly under physics constraints, while the abstract expands the evaluation claim to three additional open-weight models and explicitly announces code release.

C2.justification: v7 substantially qualifies applicability and workflow conclusions: Besiege is described as a controlled testbed rather than a direct manufacturing proxy, and five-role workflow superiority is limited by task/model dependence. It also attributes one-shot degradation to imitation bias and simple constructions to task formulation, while interpreting analyst-assisted recovery as feasible but unreliable. These add substantive boundaries and mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: v5 provides a project-page link; v7 adds an explicit code-release statement and direct repository link. It also supplies additional model identifiers, full experimental prompts in Appendix J, fidelity-check procedures, and Figure 8 normalization/binning details. Existing implementation documentation is retained, although J.2 inconsistently specifies five substructures and only one.

R1.justification: The El-Rayes and Khalafallah (2005) citation is removed with the part-minimization rationale. Otherwise, the cited research and Appendix A comparisons, including positioning against BesiegeField, are retained. Publication updates for works such as ToolLLM, VOYAGER, and GeoGramBench do not introduce new cited works.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the original task/agent prompts are retained. Local rewrites clarify workflow justification, evaluation, and limitations; model comparison receives its own subsection, Appendix F is reorganized, and an impact statement and Appendix J are added. Author affiliations and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: v7 replaces the single-column main text with a two-column conference layout, substantially relocating and resizing existing displays. It adds three experimental tables and two figures for complex bridges and fidelity measurements, expands Figure 8's caption, and redistributes retained appendix tables. These are extensive visual changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v7 strengthens the benchmark through quantitative library validation, broader model comparisons, additional diagnostic experiments, and clearer reproducibility information. Its narrower claims about manufacturing applicability and workflow superiority also improve calibration. The gains remain limited: fidelity is checked on one machine, the prompting study covers two models on one task, and the new complex-bridge prompt contains conflicting substructure requirements. These additions provide a useful net improvement while leaving the central benchmark and original results largely unchanged.
